objectives: Two new relative pairs: B major with G♯ minor, and D♭ major with B♭ minor
B major has five sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯); D♭ major has five flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭)
G♯ minor completes the sharp minor keys and B♭ minor the flat minor keys at this grade

concept.title: Grade 4 keys
concept.body: Two more major keys arrive, each with five accidentals, and each brings its relative minor. B major has five sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯) and pairs with G♯ minor; D♭ major has five flats (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭) and pairs with B♭ minor. The relative minor's tonic still sits a minor 3rd below its major partner — count down from B to G♯, and from D♭ to B♭.

teach.smartTip: Count three semitones — a minor 3rd — down from the major tonic to find the relative minor: B down to G♯, D♭ down to B♭.
teach.didYouKnow: B major and D♭ major sit right next to each other on the piano — B major's tonic and C♭ (D♭ major's leading note) are the same key — yet their key signatures are opposites: five sharps versus five flats.

objectives: Name a major key by counting the sharps or flats in its signature
B major has five sharps; D♭ major has five flats
Five is one more than the four you met at Grade 3 — the count is the whole difference

concept.title: Counting to five
concept.body: Grade 3 took you to four accidentals: E major with four sharps, A♭ major with four flats. Grade 4 adds one more of each. B major has five sharps; D♭ major has five flats. Telling sharps from flats is only half the job — you have to count them exactly, because a single accidental is the whole difference between B major and E major, or between D♭ major and A♭ major. The order never varies, so the fifth symbol is always the one that tells you which of the pair you are looking at.

teach.smartTip: Count first, then decide: five sharps is B major, four is E major; five flats is D♭ major, four is A♭ major.
teach.didYouKnow: The order the sharps appear in is always the same — F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯ A♯ — so B major's fifth sharp is A♯, and reading that last sharp is a quick way to confirm the key.

lessons.title: Harmonic and melodic minor in the new keys

objectives: The harmonic and melodic minor rules you know now apply to G♯ minor and B♭ minor
G♯ harmonic minor's raised 7th is F𝄪 (F double-sharp) — the first double-sharp in the course
B♭ harmonic minor's raised 7th is A♮ — raising a flatted 7th can land back on a natural

concept.title: Harmonic and melodic minor in the new keys
concept.body: The same rules apply: harmonic minor raises the natural minor's 7th a semitone; melodic minor raises the 6th and 7th going up and reverts coming down. Spelling the raised 7th on the 7th letter forces a double-sharp in G♯ minor — its natural 7th is F♯, so raising it a semitone gives F double-sharp (F𝄪), written with the 𝄪 sign, never G natural. B♭ minor is gentler: its natural 7th is A♭, so the raised 7th is simply A♮.

teach.smartTip: Always raise on the same letter. G♯ minor's 7th letter is F, so its raised 7th must stay an F — an F♯ raised a semitone is F double-sharp, not G.
teach.didYouKnow: A double-sharp (𝄪) raises a note by two semitones — a whole tone — from its natural pitch, so F𝄪 sounds the same as G, but naming it F keeps every letter of the G♯ minor scale distinct.

objectives: A chromatic scale moves entirely in semitones, using every pitch between its tonic and the octave
That is twelve semitone steps — thirteen notes counting both the tonic and its octave
Ascending, it is spelled with sharps: a sharpened letter fills each whole-tone gap, and none is added where letters are already a semitone apart (E–F, B–C)

concept.title: The chromatic scale
concept.body: A chromatic scale climbs entirely by semitones, touching every note between the tonic and its octave — twelve steps, thirteen notes. Ascending, it is written with sharps: between two letters a whole tone apart you insert the lower letter sharpened (C, C♯, D, D♯, E …), and where two letters are already only a semitone apart — E to F, and B to C — you add nothing. The key signature plays no part: a chromatic scale carries no key of its own.

teach.smartTip: Going up, reach for sharps. Every whole-tone gap gets a sharpened note wedged in; the two natural semitones, E–F and B–C, are left alone.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Chromatic’ comes from the Greek chroma, meaning colour — the extra notes between the scale steps were heard as adding colour to the plain diatonic scale.

objectives: Every degree of a scale has a technical name, not just a number
In order: tonic (1st), supertonic (2nd), mediant (3rd), subdominant (4th), dominant (5th), submediant (6th), leading note (7th)
The tonic and dominant are the two strongest degrees; the leading note sits a semitone below the tonic and pulls up to it

concept.title: Technical names of scale degrees
concept.body: Each note of a scale has a technical name describing its role. Counting up from the tonic: tonic (1st), supertonic (2nd), mediant (3rd), subdominant (4th), dominant (5th), submediant (6th), and leading note (7th). The tonic is home and the dominant — a 5th above — is its strongest relation. ‘Mediant’ sits midway between tonic and dominant; ‘subdominant’ is a 5th below the tonic (the ‘sub’ mirroring the dominant below rather than above), and ‘submediant’ midway between tonic and subdominant going down. The leading note lies a semitone under the tonic and leads the ear back up to it.

teach.smartTip: Anchor on tonic (1) and dominant (5). Subdominant is the 4th — think of it as the dominant measured a 5th *below* the tonic instead of above.
teach.didYouKnow: The leading note earns its name from its pull: sitting just a semitone below the tonic, it sounds unfinished until it steps up to resolve — which is exactly why the harmonic minor raises it.

objectives: The breve is the longest note value at this grade — worth two semibreves, or eight crotchet beats
It is drawn as an open notehead with a short vertical line on each side (or a square notehead)
You meet it in broad, slow passages; it is rare but worth recognising

concept.title: The breve
concept.body: The breve is the longest note value you'll meet — worth two semibreves, or eight crotchet beats. It is drawn as an open (hollow) notehead flanked by a short vertical line on each side, sometimes as a square notehead instead. Because it lasts so long, it only fits bars with room for it — you'll see it in slow, broad music rather than busy passages.

teach.smartTip: A breve is two semibreves joined — eight crotchet beats in all, twice the length of a semibreve.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Breve’ comes from the Latin brevis, ‘short’ — it was once one of the shortest notes in medieval music, before quicker values pushed it all the way to the long end of the scale.

objectives: The breve rest is the longest rest — a silence lasting eight beats, as long as the breve note
It is drawn as a solid block filling the space between the middle two lines of the stave
A breve rest lasts twice as long as a semibreve rest, just as a breve lasts twice a semibreve

concept.title: The longest silence
concept.body: Just as the breve is the longest note, the breve rest is the longest rest — eight crotchet beats, twice the four of a semibreve rest. It sits as a solid block between the middle two lines of the stave, filling the whole space rather than hanging from a line like the semibreve rest. To complete a long bar, count the beats already used and match the gap: a full eight-beat gap calls for the breve rest.

teach.smartTip: Two semibreve rests make a breve rest — eight beats of silence. The block fills the middle space; the semibreve rest only hangs beneath a line.
teach.didYouKnow: The breve rest is so rare that many musicians go years without writing one — it turns up mostly in slow music with very long bars.

objectives: A first dot adds half the note's value; a second dot adds half again — half of the first dot
A double-dotted note therefore lasts one and three-quarter times its plain value
Example: a double-dotted minim = minim + crotchet + quaver = three and a half crotchet beats

concept.title: Double-dotted notes
concept.body: A single dot adds half the note's value. A second dot adds half again — but half of the FIRST dot, not the note. So a double-dotted note lasts one and three-quarter times its plain value. A double-dotted minim is minim + crotchet + quaver (2 + 1 + ½ = 3½ crotchet beats); a double-dotted crotchet is crotchet + quaver + semiquaver. Each dot is worth half of whatever sits immediately to its left.

teach.smartTip: First dot = half the note; second dot = half the first dot (a quarter of the note). Add them up: 1 + ½ + ¼ = 1¾ of the plain value.
teach.didYouKnow: Double dots make a dotted rhythm crisper — the following short note becomes even shorter and snappier. Baroque overtures and marches lean on this for their dignified, pointed feel.

objectives: A duplet is two notes played in the time of three of the same value
It belongs to compound time, where the beat normally divides into three
A duplet fills one compound beat (a dotted crotchet) with two equal notes instead of three

concept.title: Duplets
concept.body: In compound time the beat divides into three. A duplet borrows one beat for TWO equal notes instead — two played in the time of three. It is written with a bracket and a small ‘2’ over the group. So in 6/8, a duplet fills one dotted-crotchet beat with two notes where three quavers would normally go. It is the mirror image of the triplet you'd meet in simple time.

teach.smartTip: A duplet is a triplet turned inside out: two-in-the-time-of-three in compound time, where a triplet is three-in-the-time-of-two in simple time.
teach.didYouKnow: A duplet lets a composer slip a momentary ‘simple-time’ feel into a compound-time bar — two even beats where the metre expects a lilting three — without changing the time signature.

objectives: The top number names the beats; the bottom number names the note that gets one beat
6, 9 and 12 on top mean compound time — group the beats in threes
The bottom number never decides simple versus compound: 6/4, 6/8 and 6/16 are all compound duple

concept.title: Reading any time signature
concept.body: To classify a time signature, read the top number first. 2, 3 or 4 means simple time — that many beats, each dividing into two. 6, 9 or 12 means compound time — group the beats in threes, so 6/8 is TWO dotted-crotchet beats, not six. The bottom number only says which note gets the beat: 8 the quaver, 4 the crotchet, 16 the semiquaver. It never changes simple versus compound — 6/4, 6/8 and 6/16 are all compound duple, just written in bigger or smaller note values.

teach.smartTip: Top number first: 2/3/4 is simple, 6/9/12 is compound (divide by three for the beat count). The bottom number is only which note gets the beat.
teach.didYouKnow: Fast movements are sometimes written in 6/16 so the page looks less crowded, while slow, broad music may use 6/4 — but both are still a lilting compound duple, exactly like 6/8.

objectives: The rule never changes: one beamed group per beat
In 2/8 and 4/8 the quaver is the beat, so semiquavers beam in pairs
In 6/4 the dotted minim is the beat, so quavers beam in sixes

concept.title: One rule, any denominator
concept.body: Grade 4 opens metres with quaver and minim beats, and the grouping rule survives all of them unchanged: one beamed group per beat. In 2/8 and 4/8 the beat is a quaver, so semiquavers beam in pairs and each pair is a beat. In 6/4 the beat is a dotted minim, three crotchets long, so a bar of quavers beams as two groups of six. The groups get longer or shorter, but a reader still counts beats by counting beams. Work out the beat from the time signature, then beam that much and break.

teach.smartTip: Find the beat, then beam exactly one beat at a time. The denominator alone never tells you.
teach.didYouKnow: 6/4 was standard in Renaissance dance music and came back through Holst and Stravinsky, who liked its long, slow-turning beat.

objectives: Name the interval between ANY two notes now, not only above the tonic
A perfect or major interval made a semitone wider is augmented; a perfect or minor interval made a semitone narrower is diminished
The augmented 4th (e.g. F up to B) and diminished 5th (B up to F) are the classic examples — both span six semitones

concept.title: Augmented and diminished intervals
concept.body: Two new qualities join perfect, major and minor. Widen a perfect or major interval by a semitone and it becomes AUGMENTED; narrow a perfect or minor interval by a semitone and it becomes DIMINISHED. Find the number first by counting letter names (F–G–A–B is a 4th), then the quality by the semitones. The most common examples are the augmented 4th (F up to B, six semitones) and the diminished 5th (B up to F, also six semitones) — the same distance on the keyboard, named differently by how the notes are spelled. You can now name intervals between any two notes, not just from the key's tonic.

teach.smartTip: Number first (count letter names), quality second (count semitones). Bigger than perfect/major = augmented; smaller than perfect/minor = diminished.
teach.didYouKnow: The augmented 4th and diminished 5th — the ‘tritone’ — was once nicknamed diabolus in musica, ‘the devil in music’, for its restless sound that seems to demand resolution.

objectives: The alto (C) clef is a third clef, alongside treble and bass
Its middle line is middle C (C4) — everything else is read from there
It is the viola's everyday clef, keeping that instrument's music on the staff

concept.title: The alto clef
concept.body: The alto clef — also called the C clef — centres on middle C: its middle line IS middle C (C4). It is the viola's everyday clef, keeping that instrument's music on the staff without a forest of ledger lines. Read it like any clef: find middle C on the centre line, then count lines and spaces up or down. The bottom line is F3 and the top line is G4.

teach.smartTip: The two curved arms of the alto clef point straight at the middle line — and that line is middle C. Count every other note from there.
teach.didYouKnow: The alto clef is a movable ‘C clef’: the same symbol shifted up one line becomes the tenor clef (for high cello and bassoon). Sitting on the middle line, it is the alto clef the viola reads.

lessons.title: Octave transposition to and from the alto clef

objectives: Rewrite a melody an octave higher or lower, moving between clefs so it stays on the staff
Every letter name stays the same — only the octave (and the clef) changes
Moving to a higher clef writes the melody up an octave; to a lower clef, down an octave

concept.title: Octave transposition to and from the alto clef
concept.body: Octave transposition rewrites a melody an octave away while keeping every letter name the same — only the octave changes. Choosing a different clef lets the rewritten melody stay comfortably on the staff: a melody in the alto clef can be written an octave higher in the treble, or an octave lower in the bass. The notes look different on the page, but they are the same letters, just an octave apart.

teach.smartTip: Same letters, new octave. Moving to a higher clef (alto → treble) shifts the tune up an octave; to a lower clef (alto → bass), down an octave.
teach.didYouKnow: Rewriting the same music in another clef and octave is how a viola line might be shared with a violinist or cellist — the clef and octave move, but the tune stays unmistakably the same.

lessons.title: The same pitch in different clefs

objectives: One sounding pitch is written at a different line or space in each clef
Middle C sits below the treble staff, above the bass staff, and on the middle line of the alto clef — three positions, one note
To rewrite a note in another clef, keep the pitch exactly and find where it lives on the new staff

concept.title: One pitch, three staves
concept.body: A clef fixes which pitch each line and space stands for, so the SAME sounding note lands in a different place depending on the clef. Middle C is the clearest case: it hangs on a ledger line just below the treble staff, on a ledger line just above the bass staff, and squarely on the middle line of the alto clef — one pitch, three positions. Rewriting a melody from one clef to another does not change a single sound; you keep every pitch and rhythm exactly, and only re-read where each note sits on the new staff.

teach.smartTip: The note does not move — you do. Keep the exact pitch and ask “where does this sound live on the new clef?”
teach.didYouKnow: This is why an orchestral score stacks different clefs: a cellist reading bass clef and a violist reading alto clef can play the very same note, each written where it sits most cleanly on their own staff.

lessons.title: Primary triads: I, IV and V

objectives: The three primary triads — I, IV and V — are built on the 1st, 4th and 5th degrees of a major scale
In a major key all three are major triads: a root, the note a 3rd above it, and the note a 5th above
Name a chord by finding which scale degree its lowest note — the root — sits on: tonic → I, subdominant → IV, dominant → V

concept.title: Primary triads: I, IV and V
concept.body: A triad is a three-note chord: a root, the note a 3rd above it, and the note a 5th above. The three PRIMARY triads are built on the most important degrees of the scale — I on the tonic (1st), IV on the subdominant (4th), and V on the dominant (5th). In a major key all three are major triads. To name a chord you see, find its lowest note — the root — and work out which scale degree it lands on in the given key: root on the tonic is I, on the subdominant IV, on the dominant V. In C major that makes I = C–E–G, IV = F–A–C, and V = G–B–D.

teach.smartTip: Read the key signature, then look at the chord's lowest note. If it is the key's 1st degree the chord is I, the 4th degree IV, the 5th degree V.
teach.didYouKnow: I, IV and V are called the primary triads because between them they use every note of the major scale — which is why so much music can be harmonised with just these three chords.

objectives: Ornaments are small signs that decorate a note with extra, quicker notes
Six to recognise: trill, turn, upper mordent, lower mordent, acciaccatura, appoggiatura
A trill shakes rapidly with the note above; a mordent flicks once; a turn curls around the note; grace notes (acciaccatura, appoggiatura) are tiny notes printed before the main one

concept.title: Ornaments
concept.body: Ornaments decorate a note with extra, faster notes, written as small signs. A TRILL (tr) shakes rapidly between the written note and the one above it. A TURN curls around the note — the note above, the note, the note below, and back. An UPPER MORDENT flicks quickly up to the note above and back; a LOWER MORDENT flicks down to the note below and back. Two are grace notes, printed small just before the main note: an ACCIACCATURA (with a slash through its stem) is crushed in as fast as possible, while an APPOGGIATURA (no slash) leans on the beat and borrows time from the main note.

teach.smartTip: A mordent flicks once (up = upper, down = lower); a turn curls both ways around the note; a trill shakes on and on. The two grace notes sit before the main note — the slashed acciaccatura is the quicker.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Acciaccatura’ comes from the Italian acciaccare, ‘to crush’ — it is crushed against the main note so fast the two almost sound at once, then instantly released.

objectives: The orchestra is grouped into four families: strings, woodwind, brass, and percussion
Instruments read the clef that fits their range — the viola reads the alto clef you just learned
Playing directions tell the player how to play: arco (with the bow), pizzicato (plucked), con sordino (with the mute)

concept.title: Instruments of the orchestra
concept.body: Orchestral instruments fall into four families. STRINGS (violin, viola, cello, double bass) are bowed or plucked. WOODWIND (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon) are blown. BRASS (trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba) are blown through a cupped mouthpiece. PERCUSSION (such as the timpani) are struck. Each instrument reads the clef that best fits its range: the violin and flute read treble, the cello and double bass read bass, and the viola reads the alto clef — which is why you learned it. Composers also write playing directions telling the player how to sound a note: arco means 'with the bow', pizzicato 'plucked', and con sordino 'with the mute'.

teach.smartTip: Four families: strings, woodwind, brass, percussion. The viola is the string instrument that reads the alto clef — that is exactly why the alto clef was worth learning.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Pizzicato’ is Italian for ‘pinched’ — the player plucks the string with a fingertip instead of drawing the bow across it, giving a short, bright, detached note.

objectives: Read a passage drawn from the full Grade 4 vocabulary
Keep the reading order steady when there is more on the page
Answer questions that mix pitch, rhythm and metre

concept.title: More on the page, same method
concept.body: Grade 4 adds double dots, duplets, new metres and a wider set of keys, and a passage may use any of them. That makes the page busier rather than the questions harder, and the danger is reading in the wrong order: a learner who looks at the notes before the key signature will name the wrong pitch every time an accidental is implied. Keep the order. Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. If a question asks about a bar, count the bars from the beginning rather than estimating — an examiner's answer is always exact, and a passage with an anacrusis does not start at bar one.

teach.smartTip: Clef, key signature, time signature, then notes. The same order every time.
teach.didYouKnow: Examiners write the general-observation question last, after the rest of the paper is set, so that it uses only what the paper has already asked about.

objectives: Two notes are enharmonic when they sound the same pitch but are spelled with different letters
Every black key on the keyboard has two names — one sharp, one flat
F♯ and G♭ are the same sound written two ways; so are C♯/D♭, D♯/E♭, G♯/A♭ and A♯/B♭

concept.title: The same pitch, two spellings
concept.body: On a keyboard the black key between F and G can be called F♯ (a semitone above F) or G♭ (a semitone below G). Same key, same sound — two names. Notes related this way are called enharmonic equivalents. Which spelling you use depends on the key you are in: sharp keys prefer sharps, flat keys prefer flats. The five black keys give the five common pairs: C♯/D♭, D♯/E♭, F♯/G♭, G♯/A♭ and A♯/B♭.

teach.smartTip: Keep the pitch, change the letter: an enharmonic equivalent always uses the neighbouring letter name — F♯ becomes G♭, never F♭.
teach.didYouKnow: On a piano the two spellings are the exact same key, but a string or voice can bend them apart a hair — many musicians play a G♭ a touch lower than an F♯, so the two names carry a subtly different feel.

objectives: A double sharp (𝄪) raises a note by two semitones — a whole tone above the natural
A double flat (𝄫) lowers a note by two semitones — a whole tone below the natural
Name one by its letter plus “double sharp” or “double flat”: F𝄪 is “F double sharp”, not G

concept.title: Raising and lowering by a whole tone
concept.body: You already met a double sharp inside a scale: the raised 7th of G♯ harmonic minor is F𝄪. A double sharp (written 𝄪, sometimes an ×) raises the letter by two semitones — F𝄪 sounds the same as G, but it is still spelled as an F because the key needs it that way. A double flat (written 𝄫) lowers by two semitones, so B𝄫 sounds like A. Keep the letter, name the accidental: F𝄪 is “F double sharp”, never “G”.

teach.smartTip: Keep the letter name and add the words: a double sharp on F is still an F — “F double sharp” — even though it sounds like G.
teach.didYouKnow: Double sharps appear whenever a key already full of sharps needs to raise a note further — like the F𝄪 leading note of G♯ minor. Composers keep the letter so the note still reads as the seventh degree of the scale, not a stray G.
